summary: Defines SUA, a protocol that carries Signalling Connection Control Part user messages, used in telephone signalling, over IP using the Stream Control Transmission Protocol. It is modular and symmetric, so it works in several architectures, including signalling gateways.

plainLanguage.summary: Phone company networks have their own signal language. This document shows how to carry those signals inside regular internet traffic.

questions: what is the sccp user adaptation layer
subtitle: How to carry telephone-network SCCP user signalling over IP, using SCTP as the transport.

tldr.problem: Telephone networks use SS7 signalling, and its SCCP users such as TCAP and RANAP need to talk to IP-based systems like databases and call controllers.
tldr.mechanism: SUA adapts SCCP-user messages into a message format of its own, with a common header and tag-length-value parameters, and carries them over SCTP between a Signalling Gateway and IP signalling nodes, or between two IP nodes.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that is not marked as obsoleted or updated. It supports both gateway and peer-to-peer designs, with fail-over between Application Server Processes.

today: RFC 3868 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2004, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of SUA as written here.

sections.title: What SUA Is For
sections.content:
RFC 3868 defines the SCCP User Adaptation Layer (SUA). It transports the messages of any Signalling Connection Control Part (SCCP) user over IP using the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP, RFC 2960). SCCP users include TCAP, with the MAP and CAP protocols on top of it, and RANAP.

The scope covers SCCP connectionless service, SCCP connection-oriented service, management of the SCTP associations between gateways and IP-based nodes, distributed IP-based signalling nodes, and asynchronous reporting of status changes to management. The protocol is designed to be modular and symmetric, so it fits both a gateway to an IP endpoint design and a peer-to-peer IP design.

SUA supports all four SCCP protocol classes transparently. Classes 0 and 1 make up the connectionless service (class 1 adds sequenced delivery). Classes 2 and 3 make up the connection-oriented service (class 3 adds flow control).
sections.plainLanguage: Old phone networks and the internet speak different languages. SUA lets the machines that run phone services talk over the internet without changing what they say.

sections.title: Gateways, Servers and Peers
sections.content:
The RFC names the roles. A Signalling Gateway (SG) sits at the border of the SS7 and IP networks and relays SCCP-user signalling to IP endpoints. An Application Server (AS) is a logical entity serving a specific Routing Key, for example a virtual IP database. It contains one or more Application Server Processes (ASPs), of which one or more normally process traffic. An IP Server Process (IPSP) is like an ASP but uses SUA peer to peer, without a gateway.

Three architectures are shown. For connectionless transport, SCCP and SUA meet in the SG. The SG may act as the endpoint, where messages are routed on point code and subsystem number, or as a relay point, where a Global Title translation picks the Application Server. For connection-oriented transport, the SG ties together the two connection sections between the SS7 endpoint and the ASP. In the all-IP architecture, two IPSPs talk directly and no gateway is needed.

A Routing Key describes the set of SS7 parameters that selects traffic for one Application Server. Routing Keys are mutually exclusive, so a message cannot match more than one. A Routing Context value identifies the matching Application Server in messages, and it maps 1:1 to a Routing Key within an AS.
sections.plainLanguage: The gateway is a border guard between two countries. It checks each letter's address and hands it to the right office inside, and the offices can also swap letters directly with each other.

sections.title: Messages and Parameters
sections.content:
Every SUA message starts with a Common Message Header: a Version field, a Reserved field, a Message Class, a Message Type and a 32-bit Message Length, followed by parameters. The only version is 1, SUA version 1.0. The Reserved field is set to 0 on sending and ignored on receipt. Message Length counts the header, the parameters and all padding.

Parameters use a Tag-Length-Value format: a 16-bit tag, a 16-bit length and a value. A parameter's total length must be a multiple of 4 bytes, so senders pad with zero bytes, which the length field does not count and receivers ignore. An optional parameter may occur at most once in a message. The receiver should accept parameters in any order unless the RFC mandates otherwise.

The data part of an SUA message carries the SCCP-user data, not an encapsulated SCCP message. For connectionless transfer, the CLDT message carries mandatory Routing Context, Protocol Class, Source Address, Destination Address, Sequence Control and Data parameters, and optional SS7 Hop Count, Importance, Message Priority, Correlation ID and Segmentation. It covers the SCCP UDT, XUDT and LUDT messages. CLDR reports errors when return on error is set. Connection-oriented messages include CORE, COAK, COREF, RELRE, RELCO, RESRE, RESCO, CODT, CODA, COERR and COIT.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message is an envelope with a label on the front saying what kind of message it is and how long it is. Inside are small labelled notes, each padded to fit neat 4-byte slots.

sections.title: ASP and AS States
sections.content:
The SG tracks the state of every ASP in every Application Server. An ASP is in one of three states: ASP-DOWN (the peer is unavailable or the SCTP association is down, and every ASP starts here), ASP-INACTIVE (available but application traffic is stopped) or ASP-ACTIVE (traffic is flowing). The ASP drives the changes with ASP Up, ASP Active, ASP Inactive and ASP Down messages, each acknowledged. The ASP is always the initiator of ASP Up, and it must wait for the ASP Up Ack before sending other SUA messages. If an active ASP is overridden by another ASP in the AS, it falls back to inactive.

An AS has four states: AS-DOWN, AS-INACTIVE, AS-ACTIVE (at least one ASP is active) and AS-PENDING. AS-PENDING is entered when the last active ASP goes inactive or down. A recovery timer T(r) starts and the SG queues incoming messages. If an ASP becomes active before it expires, the queued messages go to that ASP. Otherwise the SG may discard them, and the AS moves to AS-INACTIVE if some ASP is inactive, or to AS-DOWN if not.

For IPSPs, an implementation that supports IPSP communication MUST support the Single Exchange model (one request and acknowledgement changes state) and MAY implement the Double Exchange model (both sides send requests and acknowledge).
sections.plainLanguage: A worker is either off duty, on standby, or working. The team is working if at least one person is working, and if the last one leaves, the boss waits a moment holding the mail before deciding what to do.

sections.title: Routing, Streams and Fail-over
sections.content:
At the SG, the message distribution function compares incoming SS7 traffic with provisioned Routing Keys to find the Application Server, then picks an ASP in the ASP-ACTIVE state. If several are active, traffic is load-shared, for example round robin. In Broadcast Mode every active ASP gets a copy. Routing keys can be provisioned (for example by a MIB) or registered dynamically with Registration Request and Response messages. A default treatment for unmatched traffic may be set, or the message dropped with notice to management.

SUA uses SCTP stream 0 for management messages. Protocol class 0 may use unordered delivery. Classes 1, 2 and 3 MUST use ordered delivery, and data messages MUST NOT go on stream 0 when there is more than one stream. Load sharing must keep the later messages of a TCAP transaction or SCCP connection going to the same ASP that saw the first one. For this, ASPs may supply load-sharing labels in the TID or DRN parameter.

A relay function can pick the next-hop SCTP association based on Global Title, hostname, IP address or point code. To prevent loops, an SS7 hop counter starts at a maximum of 15 or less and is decremented at each relay. At zero, return or refusal procedures run with reason Hop counter violation. Optional Heartbeat messages can detect loss of the transport. A peer that hears nothing within 2*T(beat) is considered unavailable.
sections.plainLanguage: The gateway sorts mail to the right team and spreads it fairly among whoever is on duty. Mail from one conversation always goes to the same person, and a countdown on each letter stops it from circling forever.

sections.title: Port, Payload ID and Timers
sections.content:
IANA assigned SCTP Payload Protocol Identifier 4 to SUA. It SHOULD be put in each SCTP DATA chunk. The value 0 (unspecified) is also allowed, and no other value may be used. IANA registered SCTP port 14001 for SUA, and SGPs are recommended to listen on it, though they MAY use statically configured ports.

New message classes, message types and parameters are assigned by IANA through IETF Consensus. A received message type that is not supported MUST be answered with an Error message with code Unsupported Message Type.

The RFC lists default timers: Ta, Tr and T(ack) at 2 seconds, T(ias) at 7 minutes, T(iar) at 15 minutes and T(beat) at 30 seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: SUA has its own front door number so that the right program answers, and a tag on each parcel saying who it belongs to. The timers say how long to wait before asking again.

sections.title: Security
sections.content: The RFC's security section is short. It states that the security considerations in RFC 3788, Security Considerations for Signaling Transport (SIGTRAN) Protocols, apply to this document, and it adds no mechanisms of its own.
sections.plainLanguage: SUA does not add its own locks. It points to another document that explains how to keep this kind of signalling safe.
